topic: Serbia's student protest movement is about to form a government

sources.title: Who could lead Serbia next? Meet the key candidates on the student movement's list
sources.text:
After a leaderless student-led protest movement swept Serbia's former President Aleksandar Vucic from power in a historic snap election on Sunday, the country is waiting to hear who it will appoint as prime minister and to other key ministerial positions as it forms a government.
Here are some of the prominent candidates on the students' list.
FORMER CENTRAL BANK GOVERNOR DEJAN SOSKIC, 59
Dejan Soskic, an economist and professor at the University of Belgrade's Faculty of Economics, served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012, before resigning in protest at legislative amendments that he argued compromised the institution's independence. He has for years been a vocal opponent of Vucic's government.
Soskic, who was an avid biker in his youth but has mellowed into a softly spoken reformer, has frequently criticised the country’s institutional weaknesses under Vucic. In 2021, he said, without offering evidence, that systemic corruption in the Balkan state was more widespread than in neighbouring countries and that it was deterring domestic and foreign direct investment. Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party have repeatedly denied accusations of corruption.
Soskic says that prudent public finances will create a stable foundation for a permanent increase in wages and pensions. Pro-government media have criticised Soskic’s central bank record, accusing him of triggering the depreciation of the dinar during his tenure. Soskic has defended the depreciation as a reflection of the mandatory monetary policies of the time rather than a personal failure.
Nonetheless, during the election campaign, in order to increase export competitiveness, Soskic proposed correcting, or weakening, the exchange rate of the dinar - which is in a managed float against the euro - to make domestic goods cheaper in foreign currencies. An alternative, he suggested, would be to maintain a fixed, stronger exchange rate but lower costs by cutting wages.
CARDIOLOGIST AND PROFESSOR ILIJA SRDANOVIC, 55
Ilija Srdanovic, a practising cardiologist, professor at the University of Novi Sad Faculty of Medicine and a keen cyclist, became the student movement's lead candidate when the ballot list was finalised in September.
Srdanovic’s transition to frontline politics began during the student-led anti-corruption demonstrations, where he frequently appeared as a public speaker. The physician participated in the movement's "Guardians of the Constitution" bicycle tour across the northern Vojvodina province.
Srdanovic campaigned with the promise of a decentralised health system "at the service of citizens and based on equality for all patients". In an interview with the Belgrade-based FoNet news agency, Srdanovic said his political objective was building "a better Serbia, nothing else is important". He declined an invitation from Vucic to participate in a televised debate during the campaign.
However, some of his policies do not represent a sharp departure from some of Vucic's. He stressed the Student List position that Kosovo, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008, remains an integral part of the country. He also said that European Union integration is not a current priority and that the immediate focus for the incoming administration must remain on domestic anti-corruption reforms and national "existential survival".
FORMER BASKETBALL STAR DEJAN BODIROGA, 53
Dejan Bodiroga, the former captain of the Yugoslav national basketball team and current EuroLeague president, is one of the student movement's most prominent public speakers. He described Sunday's election as a fight "for the return of a country that has been hijacked".
The step into politics is the latest chapter in a life that has gripped the basketball-mad nation - from capturing back-to-back FIBA World Championship gold medals in 1998 and 2002 and leading the then Yugoslav team to an Olympic silver medal at the 1996 Atlanta Games to entering senior sports administration upon his retirement as a player in 2007 and being appointed as EuroLeague president in 2022.
During the election campaign, Bodiroga appeared at student rallies and took part in open-air folk dancing in rural municipalities. His fans frequently cheered him with a 1990s slogan "We have our God, his name is Bodiroga."
CHEMISTRY PROFESSOR RADOMIR SAICIC, 64
Radomir Saicic, an organic chemistry professor and a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU), was the face of the students' election win on Sunday, taking the podium at their headquarters after Vucic conceded defeat to hail the outcome as a "citizens' victory".
He is a specialist in medicinal chemistry whose research focuses on the synthesis of chemotherapy treatments and antiviral therapies, including a special COVID-19 project in collaboration with the Pasteur Institute.
Saicic joined the student-led anti-corruption protests that followed the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad. He became a target for pro-government tabloids after signing a petition with 24 other academics demanding Vucic's resignation, and in May 2026 he walked out of a SANU gallery exhibition to protest an appearance by Nikola Selakovic, the minister of culture.
During the campaign, he told crowds that Serbia was "occupied from within" and said he was ready to put "even his life" at the disposal of the student movement.
Saicic says Kosovo is a "temporarily occupied territory" and backs energy ties with Russia.
Political analysts and local media have tipped him as a contender in the presidential election which will also be triggered by Vucic's recent resignation from the post.

sources.title: Serbia's student movement toppled a political giant. Can it now govern the country?
sources.text:
By unseating longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday's election, Serbia's student protest movement did what demonstrators in other European capitals can only dream of. Now, though, comes the gritty business of governing - something neither the students nor their handpicked candidates have any experience of.
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets across the country to celebrate when Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday in a historic poll that capped two years of peaceful anti-government protests.
But as the jubilant crowd lit flares and fireworks, sang and danced, questions lingered: who will emerge from this leaderless movement as prime minister, what exactly will their policies be, and can a bunch of political unknowns with no previous affiliation stick together to shore up the economy, root out graft and juggle complex international relations?
The answers will determine the political stability of Serbia, the largest economy in the Western Balkans, and its relations with China, Russia, and its largest trading partner, the European Union.
The students' victory "is likely to trigger broad institutional and policy changes centred on anti-corruption, the rule of law, and better public services. However, bureaucratic resistance to reforms and the movement’s limited governing experience could make the transition challenging," Teneo Global Research said in a report on Monday.
WINNERS, BUT CAN THEY STICK TOGETHER?
The protest movement began after 16 people died when a railway station canopy collapsed in the northern city of Novi Sad in 2024 and the student-led demonstrations called for accountability and an end to corruption.
Despite not having a figurehead, the students won widespread support, before choosing 250 academics, lawyers, doctors, actors, farmers and musicians to represent them in the election.
The movement and some of the top candidates on its list have given some idea of what it stands for, promising a domestic anti-corruption program centred on institutional overhauls.
It does not recognise Kosovo, Serbia's former southern province which declared independence in 2008, but wants to hold a referendum on Serbia's accession to the EU, with which relations have frayed in recent years.
Prominent figures include the head of the students' candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory. But there is no certainty that any of them will hold a ministerial post, and it remains to be seen whether the candidates can form a cohesive government that can agree on policy long enough to use their comfortable parliamentary majority to enact change.
"(The student movement created) such a shift in Serbia's culture; we will just have to see if it lasts," said Katarina Popovic, also a professor at the University of Belgrade.
"We just hope that there are big goals that can keep them together long enough to deconstruct the system."
REFORMING PUBLIC INSTITUTIONS
Under Serbia's constitution, the students' candidates have 90 days to form a government once parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.
Time matters, especially with a budget to pass before year-end amid growing public and private debt levels, while any attempt to end corruption will require an overhaul of the police and intelligence services and judicial reform.
State institutions require "detoxification" after 14 years of Vucic, said Bozo Prelevic, a Belgrade-based lawyer and former co-minister of the interior.
Prelevic warned that Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), will pose a strong opposition, and that the new government would have to fight its corner.
Vucic and the SNS repeatedly denied accusations of repression and corruption.
INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS
In Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised Vucic, but stopped short of congratulating the students.
"We respect Russia both as a great power and as our historically important partner and, in many cases, protector," Student List representative Jovo Bakic, a sociologist and a university lecturer, told Russia’s RT Balkan TV, adding that there would be no change in Serbia's foreign policy towards Russia, including not introducing sanctions against Moscow.
Also closely watching is Ukraine, which has been an indirect beneficiary of Serbian weapons in its fight to repel Russia's four-year-long invasion.
European officials congratulated the students and said they stood ready to help the country in its fight against corruption.
"I am sure (the Student List) will find a way, just as they have so far, to choose someone capable of governing - someone who will have the privilege, but also the immense responsibility, to lead Serbia through these reforms," said Savo Manojlovic of the student-friendly Move-Change movement.

sources.title: After Vučić: Serbia’s student movement celebrates victory, but Serbia still faces deep divisions and pressure from Moscow
sources.text:
The victory of Serbia’s protest-driven student movement in the Oct. 25 snap parliamentary election triggered widespread euphoria. Many observers saw the result as a turning point that could open the way for sweeping anti-corruption reforms and a revival of the country’s European integration after 14 years of dominance by Aleksandar Vučić. But the winners’ first major test will be forming a new government, which will determine whether those promised changes can move forward. Tensions remain extremely high: new institutions cannot be created overnight, and Vučić, despite conceding defeat, has continued his campaign to discredit the student movement. He is trying to pit his opponents against both the Kremlin and Donald Trump while openly hinting that he is prepared to shift the confrontation into the streets.
For years, Vučić remained Serbia’s dominant political figure regardless of the office he formally held. But after the Oct. 25 election, he lost his status as the country’s unquestioned leader: His gamble of leaving the presidency early in an attempt to return as prime minister failed. For the first time since 2012, he holds no official state position. The victory of the protest movement’s Student List, which won a majority in Serbia’s 250-seat National Assembly — the Skupština — deprived him of the ability to form a government. And under Serbian law, he cannot run again for president after voluntarily leaving that office.
“Sirens, songs, and tears of joy. What happened on Serbia’s streets showed just how much of a burden Aleksandar Vučić had become for the citizens of his own country. People’s faces showed relief, as though they had thrown off shackles and could walk freely again. No one organized this joy. There were no buses, handouts, or lists needed. It came after the man who captured the state and turned the daily humiliation of citizens into a method of government admitted defeat. We are tired of a state where one person decides who is a patriot, who is a traitor, who is allowed to speak, and whose life should be destroyed. Now there must be accountability for violence, abuses, persecution, and public money spent to preserve one man’s personal power...” Hundreds of similar reports from Serbia have circulated around the world in recent days.
Vučić’s defeat, despite his extensive use of state resources that included near-total control over much of the media, election bodies, and the judicial system reminded many of events in the fall of 2000, when mass protests brought down the regime of Slobodan Milošević.
Media outlets and experts have also drawn comparisons with Hungary’s former prime minister Viktor Orbán, who until recently had seemed politically untouchable. Those striking parallels, however, do not answer the central question: after power has been taken from Vučić, can it be retained? The atmosphere is tense, and people want swift justice. But institutions cannot be created and reformed quickly, analysts caution.
Musical chairs gone wrong
For Vučić, the risky “seat-switching maneuver” was essentially the only option left after nearly two years of mass protests, which erupted following the deaths of 16 people at the Novi Sad railway station. Growing public anger could not be suppressed either by accusations that students were terrorists or by the alleged use of a “sound weapon” against protesters.
In the past, Vučić had repeatedly turned to snap elections to reaffirm his dominance and overwhelm familiar opponents from Serbia’s traditional liberal opposition. But the decentralized student movement, with little political experience and no well-known leaders, proved much harder to defeat.
Running under the slogan “Serbia or the Mafia,” the students absorbed much of the electorate. At the same time, they refused to cooperate with opposition parties, arguing that those parties were themselves part of Serbia’s entrenched political system.
A presidential election is also due in the coming months, and Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, will try to advance its own candidate. The task will be difficult: The former president’s personal ability to control domestic political processes and the state apparatus has been sharply diminished, while the protest movement has reached the Republic Electoral Commission itself. Several commission members accused the body of pressure and dishonesty and demanded an apology over the failure to open enough polling stations abroad, forcing many voters to travel hundreds of kilometers to cast ballots.
Will Vučić delay the transfer of power?
In the Oct. 25 election, the Student List — Students Win movement received 52.54% of the vote, giving it about 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament. Vučić’s United Serbia coalition received 39.29%, goog for 103 seats. The remaining seven seats went to parties representing national minorities.
All other political forces, including the Socialist Party, Vučić’s longtime coalition partner, failed to cross the 3% parliamentary threshold. It was the first time in 30 years that the Socialists — led until 2000 by Slobodan Milošević and later by his former spokesman Ivica Dačić — failed to win parliamentary representation.
The protest movement’s victory has opened a window of opportunity, but it is not exactly a wide one. The winners have no experience governing the country, while state institutions remain under the influence of Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party. Candidates for prime minister and other cabinet posts have not yet been presented, and forming a government could take months.
Candidates for prime minister and Cabinet posts have not yet been presented, and forming Serbia’s new government could take months
Vučić’s team could also delay the transfer of power, creating the risk of a deeper crisis. Vučić, for his part, has accepted no personal responsibility for the state of the country. He blamed his defeat on independent media, unnamed European countries, and the “American deep state.”
After Oct. 25, Vučić’s political influence shifted from near-absolute dominance to opposition leadership. He still heads a large parliamentary bloc and can count on the loyalty of a substantial share of voters. His rapid concession surprised many and may have been a tactical move intended to reduce his immediate risks and preserve a political future for himself and his allies.
Vučić’s associates have already promoted claims of supposed “revolutionary terror” and a “witch hunt” aimed at eliminating him. In reality, no member of Vučić’s team has been physically attacked, arrested, or placed on a wanted list. Demands for the dismissal of senior officials who served the old system hardly match such sweeping claims. Even after the election, acting president Ana Brnabić, a Vučić ally, appeared confident enough to trade insults with passersby on the streets — and even to challenge them to arrest her.
There are, however, more prominent potential targets for investigation. The allegations against Vučić himself and Finance Minister Siniša Mali include abuse of office, corruption, financial wrongdoing, and unlawful pardons, among other matters. One of the most politically explosive cases reaching the highest levels is the investigation into the reconstruction of the Novi Sad railway station — where the fatal collapse that sparked the protest movement occurred.
Another major corruption controversy centers on the removal of cultural heritage protections from the former Yugoslav General Staff complex in Belgrade, which was bombed by NATO in 1999. The move was made to clear the way for a hotel project backed by Jared Kushner; however, Trump’s son-in-law withdrew from the $500 million project amid the controversy, and an investigation into alleged document falsification involving Culture Minister Nikola Selaković remains open.

sources.title: From Bangladesh To Serbia: Student-Led Movements Lead To Changes In Political Landscapes
sources.text:
- Student List wins Serbia snap parliamentary elections.
- President Vucic concedes defeat after long rule.
- Victory follows protests over corruption, public safety.
Serbia Election: Serbia’s political landscape on Monday reached a major turning point after President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in the snap parliamentary elections. The student-backed Student List is projected to win between 135 and 140 seats, compared with around 105 for the ruling Serbian Progressive Party. Final results are still awaited.
After the announcement, thousands of people celebrated in Belgrade. The result is significant as it marks a major challenge to a political leadership that has held power for years in Serbia and also focuses attention on student-led movements worldwide.
How The Movement Began?
The student-led movement began after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. The tragedy raised serious questions about public safety, construction standards and government accountability. Students demanded answers and action against those responsible. As the protests grew, their demands expanded and also included corruption and weak public institutions.
  BREAKING NEWS: Students in Serbia have voted out their authoritarian leadership by winning the country's parliamentary election. They started with months of student protests against corruption and have translated street mobilisation into electoral legitimacy. https://t.co/Egj29ffIft
— Rinu Oduala 🔥🔫 (@SavvyRinu) October 25, 2026
They turned it into a mass movement by organising open assemblies and not just relying on a single leader. After months of protests, the students then developed an electoral platform to challenge the ruling party directly. Their victory in the Serbia elections suggests that public anger over corruption and youth’s voices can move beyond the streets and reshape electoral politics.
The student-led movement will now form the next government, sidelining Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the 250-member parliament. However, it is yet not clear how the Student List candidate Radimir Sicic and other leaders of the movement plan to move ahead.
Recommended For You
Student Protests Becoming Political Force?
Serbia’s political shake up shows that young people are increasingly taking the lead in protests against corruption, poor governance and a lack of accountability. Recently, France also witnessed a student-led protest over poor facilities. The protests intensified after people from all walks joined it to protest against rising living costs. One of the reasons why student-led movements have found prominence is their active presence on social media, a platform that helps them share information, organise demonstrations, and bring together people from different backgrounds.
It is also observed that the movement which begins with one specific demand grows further when people see the same problem as part of a wider failure of government. However, turning public anger into lasting political change remains difficult in most cases. It becomes challenging when movements have to agree on leadership and decide the future course.
A Look At Bangladesh's Regime Change
Bangladesh is one of the powerful examples of how student-led movements can alter the political landscape of any country. In 2024, student protests in Dhaka initially focused on the civil service job quota system. However, it soon turned into widespread anger over government policies, and political repression drew more people into the streets.
The demonstrations developed into a wider uprising and led to violence across Bangladesh as protesters demanded accountability. As the protests turned violent and uncontrollable, Awami League leader Sheikh Hasina, who had been in power for 15 years, had to flee the country in August 2024.
What These Movements Tell
Serbia and Bangladesh episodes serve as a powerful reminder that when authorities fail to answer public concerns, even a small grievance can develop into a big movement, bringing political changes. Building accountable institutions, maintaining unity and delivering promises should remain a priority of the government.

sources.title: 2026 French student protests
sources.text:
Demonstrations and protests against poor economic and school conditions by workers and lycée (high school) students have taken place in France since September 2026. In early October, the protests developed into a nationwide mobilization involving students, teachers, parents, political organizations, the yellow vests and trade unions, with an estimated 550,000–800,000 people participating nationwide.
Labour movements emerged in mid-September in reaction to the cost-of-living and fuel crisis caused by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab Strait, spearheaded by a newly revived yellow vests movement. Causes also included high inflation, housing, economic stagnation, social inequality and unemployment, coupled with austerity measures and social spending cuts resulting from the public debt crisis.
Soon after, teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and limited public investment in social programs and infrastructure sparked immense students protests nationwide. Students noted stress linked to the university application website Parcoursup and high temperatures in classrooms that reached up to 40 °C (104 °F) during the 2026 European heatwaves. Despite forming separately, the protest movements converged on 17 October, along with other unrelated movements. These demonstrations are considered to be part of a wider European unrest which includes protests in Belgium, Albania, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Austria, Ireland, Serbia and Germany.
The initial police response used a variety of forceful crowd-control weapons, resulting in serious injuries, including to children. Violent conflict between police and protestors have led to 6,800 arrests, most of them of minors. The French government has accused the far-left of stirring up the unrest for political gain. Protester leaders have argued the movement is a spontaneous showing of economic grievance.
The police response drew criticism from human rights organizations like Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the UN Human Rights Office. The government rejected accusations of police repression, with Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez maintaining that the response had been proportionate in almost all cases and that some protests had turned into riots.


== Background ==


=== Economic conditions ===
In 2026, France's economy faced an unprecedented series of shocks. No economic growth occurred since the new year, shrinking by 0.2% in the first quarter, stagnating in the second quarter, and unexpectedly suffering a 0.1% decline in the third quarter of 2026. 
At the end of June, the Institut national de la statistique et des études économiques (Insee) reported government debt as €3.596 trillion ($4.08 trillion), approximately 119% of GDP, almost double the EU limit of under 60% of GDP; it is the highest in French history and third highest in the eurozone. Despite the debt crisis, deficit remained above 5% of GDP, far exceeding the EU threshold of 3%. Public spending also stood at 57% of GDP. However, it was uncovered in October that 32% of the Ministry of National Education’s budget of €28.5 billion ($32 billion) was used toward paying pensions for retirees and not education. Demographic imbalance shifted the worker-to-retiree ratio to 0.94 workers per pensioner.
Inflation accelerated while wages struggled to keep up, reaching 3.1% year-on-year in September and 3.4% by early October 2026, the highest since January 2024. Due to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab Strait in the 2026 Iran war and Yemeni civil war, the price of diesel in France rose to €2.37 per liter ($2.72 per liter) in September, just 1c below its record high of €2.38. Accommodating for the high fuel prices contributed to rising inflation and cost-of-living in the country.
Unemployment, poverty, high rent prices and government spending cuts also have motivated protestors both in France and across Europe.


=== Study conditions and government budget ===
The protests came at the start of the school year and at the same time as a public-sector strike over the government's budget plans, which include €61 billion in new spending cuts. Students cited unfilled teaching posts, overcrowded classes, long timetables and deteriorating facilities among their grievances. A 17-year-old pupil at the Lycée Paul-Éluard in Saint-Denis described temporary toilets without water, rats and cockroaches in school, and temperatures ranging from −5 °C in winter to 40 °C in summer in temporary classrooms. Another pupil described rooms with too few tables, noting that teachers had explained their own discontent before the pupils decided to join them. Ryad Rani, president of the secondary-students' union Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), cited a pupil who had gone seven months without a French teacher in a year with a French exam, and classes of 32 to 36 students; pupils elsewhere told ICI of classes of 35.
The Créteil rectorat told Agence France-Presse that demands still varied by school—teachers not replaced, class size, heavy timetables, shortages of education assistants, nurses, social workers and managers, incidents between pupils and teachers left without follow-up, and deficient undergraduate admissions web portal Parcoursup. France Info summarized what it was hearing from pupils as more resources, smaller classes, buildings in better condition, enough teachers and staff, and less stress from Parcoursup.


=== Recent protests ===
In autumn 1990, lycée students, many from working-class Paris suburbs, protested over safety, cleanliness, staffing and materials. The protests reached on the order of 100,000 people in Paris and about 150,000 nationwide. Education minister Lionel Jospin answered with an emergency plan and an increase in the education budget.
In early 2005, lycée students and their teachers mobilized against reforms to the education system made by François Fillon, and in particular against a reform of the baccalauréat that they believed would lead to greater inequalities in the value of diplomas from different schools. Between 15,000 and 40,000 students took part in the protests. Fillon backed down and announced a government amendment removing changes to the baccalauréat from the bill.
In spring 2018, opposition to the ORE law and to the new Parcoursup platform was formed mainly among university occupations. A scattering of lycée blockades took place. In the autumn, lycée students mobilized again, against Parcoursup and against Jean-Michel Blanquer's baccalauréat reform. On 11 December, hundreds of establishments were blocked or badly disrupted. Le Monde diplomatique later wrote that this map could not be explained only by the knock-on effect of the yellow vests protests, then at their height, but that the yellow vest movement was part of the context. Parcoursup was kept, with some adjustments, and the baccalauréat reform went ahead.


== Organization ==

The USL's national call, for 29 September, named four grievances: lack of teachers and staff, "dilapidated lycées", overloaded timetables and classes, and the stress caused by Parcoursup. Rani said classes sometimes held 32 to 35 pupils and asked protesters to remain peaceful. The union later called a second day on 1 October, an "act two", and a further day of action on 6 October. On RTL on 30 September, Rani said dialogue bodies run by the ministry had been "abandoned", and that it was for the minister to take the first step. Following their meeting with Education Minister Édouard Geffray on 2 October, student union leaders voiced their dissatisfaction with the government's response and called for the mobilization to continue. The USL announced further demonstrations for 6 October, with several trade-union confederations, including the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), announcing that they would join the action. Other supporting trade union confederations included the Workers' Force (FO), National Union of Autonomous Trade Unions (UNSA), French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT), Solidaires, French Confederation of Christian Workers (CFTC), and the Confédération Paysanne. The teachers' unions Unitary Trade Union Federation (FSU) and National Union of Independent Colleges and High Schools (SNALC) called for strikes and supported the protests as well.
Other lycée student unions supporting student mobilization and protests included the National High School Student Movement, the Student Union, and the "Les Lycéens!" union.


=== Participating and supporting organizations ===

The Union syndicale lycéenne and Union étudiante called for joint mobilization by secondary-school and university students on 1 October. Reporting on the demonstrations that day, Le Monde described a heterogeneous movement involving students seeking improved educational conditions as well as people involved in confrontations. It also reported that some participants were not pupils of the schools outside which they gathered.
La France Insoumise (LFI) representatives attended demonstrations. Jean-Luc Mélenchon stated that the party supported nonviolent protest and has participated in protests on 24 October.
Muslim students of France (French: Étudiants musulmans de France, EMF) also supported the mobilization. According to Le Point, the association and its local branches circulated calls for action from 5 to 9 October, while its Belfort branch had joined a demonstration alongside secondary-school students on 1 October. The magazine reported that EMF cooperated with RED Jeunes, with which it had co-founded the anti-Islamophobia collective Génération EDR in March 2025.


=== Others ===
The yellow vests movement began in 2018 as a protest against fuel taxes and the rising cost of living and has since returned as a symbol for the 2026 protests. The demonstrations lacked a single organizational leadership, yet they gave voice to diverse forms of social discontent, with grievances including cost of living, education, public spending, social inequality, and political corruption.


== Timeline ==


=== Emergence of the protests ===
On 15 September, workers, including fishermen, police officers, farmers, construction workers, energy workers, medical workers, university staff and other groups participated in demonstrations. On 17 September, fishermen took their boats and blockaded two ports in Nice and Sète, obstructing maritime traffic. Others burned tires and wooden pallets on roads to petrol depots in Frontignan, preventing access. On social media, the 2018 yellow vests movement saw a resurgence, with messages calling for a general mobilization on 17 October being shared.
Soon after the beginning of the new school year in September, several issues with the school infrastructure prompted students in French Guiana to block the Felix Éboué high school in Cayenne, denouncing poor conditions. In Mayotte, parents together with teachers and students have been blocking access to the lycee of the North of Acoua since the end of August, a movement which was "largely ignored" by mass media in metropolitan France.
In metropolitan France, the mobilization began on 21 September at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, a commune in the suburbs of Paris. The day after a teachers' strike on 17 September against lack of resources and staff, pupils organized a protest. Pupils said they felt neglected by the Ministry of National Education and cited lack of resources and staff, overcrowded classes, and rooms short of tables.
An academic source and the USL later presented that mobilization as the start of the national movement.
Contemporaneous reports, including Le Monde and a 24 September account by actu.fr, dated the spreading movement to Monday 21 September at the same lycée, where several teaching posts were unfilled. The Créteil rectorate said on 24 September that demands still varied by school.
Through 25 September the spread stayed local. Actu.fr said about 10 lycées were affected by 24 September, mainly in S

sources.title: Student List
sources.text:
The Student List (Serbian: Студентска листа, romanized: Studentska lista; abbr. SL) is an electoral list formed by the Students in Blockade, the student movement that led the anti-corruption protests following the Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse in November 2024. First announced in May 2025, after the students demanded early elections, the list consists not of students but of 250 academics, professionals and public figures selected by student plenums. The list won the 2026 Serbian parliamentary election with 53.69% of the vote and 140 of the 250 seats, an absolute majority, according to the final results announced by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) on 5 November.
The list runs as the citizens' group Student List – Students Are Winning (Студентска листа – Студенти побеђују, Studentska lista – Studenti pobeđuju), founded on 9 September 2026, the day the election was called, and was proclaimed as number 3 on the ballot. Its programme, the 11-point "Student Plan", centres on the fight against corruption and organised crime, alongside social measures in education, housing and healthcare. Several parliamentary and extra-parliamentary opposition parties withdrew from the election to back the list.


== Background ==

On 1 November 2024, the canopy of the Novi Sad railway station collapsed, killing 16 people. This triggered a wave of protests. Students who joined the protests blockaded their faculties with four demands: the publication of all documentation on the canopy's renovation, criminal accountability for those who attacked students of the Faculty of Dramatic Arts during a protest, the dropping of charges against students and demonstrators arrested at the 5 November 2024 protest in Novi Sad, and a 20% increase in university funding. A fifth and sixth demand were added in April 2025. Citing the government's failure to meet their demands, the students called for early parliamentary elections on 5 May 2025.


== Formation ==

The idea of a separate list was announced in May 2025, shortly after the call for early elections. Amid public debate about how the opposition electorate should be mobilised and whether the students should run jointly with political parties, they said they would form their own independent list, which would not include students as candidates.


=== From protest movement to electoral list ===
In the early phase of the protests, particularly until April 2025, the Students in Blockade stressed that they were not interested in elections or in who held power, and rejected coalitions or mergers with existing opposition parties. Contacts with parties were initially limited to coordinating protest demands and securing the release of detained activists, as the students sought to keep the movement above party politics. As the movement grew, the students came to be seen as the largest opposition force in the country.
Having decided to form their own list, the students entered talks with the opposition from a position of high public support. Rather than seeking places on party lists, they called on opposition parties not to run and to urge their voters to back the Student List instead. Months of talks and pressure, including appeals from the academic community and the civic initiative ProGlas, were accompanied by public disputes, such as a clash between the plenum of the Belgrade Faculty of Law and the New Democratic Party of Serbia. In September 2026, several opposition parties withdrew in favour of the Student List, while those that chose to run did not unite in a single opposition list (see Support).


=== Registration ===

The association Student List was registered with the Business Registers Agency on 21 May 2026 for a fixed term, valid until 1 May 2028. According to its Statute, it is a voluntary, non-governmental, non-partisan and non-profit association established for a fixed period to raise civic awareness of the importance of democracy and free and fair elections. Its goals include greater youth participation in democratic processes, monitoring elections and referendums, promoting the rule of law and freedom of speech, and holding those who break the law accountable.
The citizens' group Student List – Students Are Winning (SL – SP), through which the list formally contests the election, was founded on 9 September 2026, the day the snap parliamentary election was called. Its founders are:

All of the founders are also candidates on the list.


=== Decoy associations ===
Shortly before the citizens' group was founded, three associations with names closely resembling that of the list were registered: "Students Are Winning", "Student List of Serbia – Students Are Winning" and "Student List of Belgrade – Students Are Winning". According to Vreme, all three were founded on 3 September 2026 by the same individual, with identical statutes and the same address in New Belgrade. The students described them as "fake associations" and said they suspected that the government would use them to submit decoy lists bearing the Student List's name, noting that recent changes to the electoral law allowed a single voter to sign in support of more than one list. They stressed that "Student List – Students Are Winning" was their only list.


== Candidates ==


=== Selection ===
According to reports in May 2025, the selection process was to begin with students contacting potential candidates between 8 and 14 May 2025. Candidacies would then be submitted to faculty commissions, and candidates would present themselves to the student plenums and answer students' questions, after which a student electoral commission would hold a vote. The 250 places on the list were to be distributed among the five state universities and the colleges of applied studies roughly in proportion to their size, and the names kept secret until the elections were called.
In June 2025, the students published the conditions for candidates: they had to be adult citizens of Serbia, could not be students, and had to respect the list's programme. Each candidate also had to sign a statement declaring that they had never been a member of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), the Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) or any of 19 other parties named in it, among them the Social Democratic Party of Serbia, PUPS, the Serbian Radical Party, United Serbia and the Serbian Party Oathkeepers; that they had never been an official of a parliamentary opposition party, from member of its presidency or main board to president of a local board; that they had never been an MP, minister or state secretary on behalf of the ruling coalition; that they had never acquired illegal material gain in cooperation with SNS and SPS or by abusing a public office; and that they had no final conviction to more than a year in prison, no conviction for an offence prosecuted ex officio carrying a sentence of more than three years, and no ruling against them by a court of honour. If elected, the candidates pledged to remain in the political organisation that had nominated them and not to change parliamentary group, not to vote for proposals contrary to its programme, and to work towards fulfilling the demands of the Students in Blockade and the goals of their "Social Agreement" and "Programme Minimum"; a candidate found to have made a false declaration or to have breached these pledges would be considered to have resigned on the day this was established.
The student plenums also had the right to veto individual candidates. The secrecy surrounding the list led to extensive speculation throughout 2025 and 2026. Vladan Đokić, rector of the University of Belgrade, was frequently mentioned as a possible head of the list and said he was prepared to take part if the students chose him, but he was vetoed by a narrow majority in the plenums in September 2026. Others excluded from the list included professor Milo Lompar, prosecutor Jasmina Paunović, and activist Predrag Voštinić. The pro-government daily Politika reported that the plenums had vetoed dozens of potential candidates, which it presented as an effort to preserve the list's profile by excluding certain intellectuals and right-wing figures. Other names in media speculation included journalist Žaklina Tatalović and lawyers Zdenko Tomanović and Božo Prelević. In early September 2026, students said the full list of 250 candidates was ready and awaiting only the calling of elections.


=== Composition ===

The movement deliberately avoided appointing a conventional political leader, choosing its candidates through plenums and collective decision-making. The list is headed by cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad, and comprises 250 candidates, mostly academics, experts and public figures, including the 14 founders of the citizens' group. Other prominent candidates include Nemanja Đurić, president of the Judicial Authority Trade Union; professor Ljubica Oparnica; sociologist Jovo Bakić; political scientist Adem Mavrić; actors Tihomir Stanić and Dragan Jovanović; environmental activist Zlatko Kokanović; geologist Zoran Đajić; former basketball player and Euroleague Basketball president Dejan Bodiroga; former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić; and former athlete Mihail Dudaš.


== Campaign ==
The main principles of the students' programme were first presented at the "Slavija – You and Me" rally in Belgrade on 23 May 2026, with more detailed parts to be presented at public forums across Serbia. The campaign formally opened with a rally in Novi Sad on 10 September 2026, attended by around 6,000 people according to the Archive of Public Gatherings, at which the first 30 candidates were presented. Addressing the rally, grammar school teacher Katarina Šćepanović said that it was "the moment for togetherness, for association and solidarity among citizens".
After appealing to citizens in late August to lend premises for signature collection, the students submitted the list to the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) on 14 September, following a march through central Belgrade, with around 70,000 signatures. The full list of 250 candidates was published on the students' website the same day, with the students stating that the list has no leader. On 15 September, RIK certified 69,099 valid signatures, nearly seven times the legal threshold of 10,000, and proclaimed the list.
The students then presented their programme, the "Student Plan", on a tour of Serbia: in Vojvodina on 15 September, eastern Serbia on 16 September, western Serbia on 17 September, southern Serbia on 18 September, and Belgrade and central Serbia on 19 September.


== Programme ==
The programme was drafted over several months. In November 2025, student Vukašin Đinović said that it was being written in cooperation with experts from various fields, including farmers, doctors, teachers, social workers and cultural workers. During the campaign, some opposition parties and pro-government media called on the students to state their positions on issues such as Kosovo, Republika Srpska, European integration, economic and social policy, and foreign relations.


=== Student Plan ===
The "Student Plan", presented on 15 September 2026, consists of 11 points divided into three sections, "Serbia or the Mafia", "Knowledge is Power" and "Serbia Grows with Us". The fight against crime and corruption is at its centre, alongside social measures such as free school textbooks and cheaper medicines. Its central promise has been described as a broad change in the way Serbia is governed. The 11 points are:

1. Freeing the courts and prosecution through a Special Prosecutorial Police
A vetted police unit to investigate corruption and arrest those responsible without political obstruction, freeing judges and prosecutors from political pressure; a comprehensive review of the Ministry of the Interior, removal of officials linked to organised crime, and dismissal of police officers who broke the law in dealing wi
